_comment: Documented alternative conceptions for the gravity/free-fall topic, authored by the procedure in docs/misconception_library.md. Every persona for this topic is built on the first entry; the rest are recorded because the research was done. Ordering is by how well documented the conception is. Citations live in gravity.sources.md. Note the topic's question is essentially verbatim Force Concept Inventory item 1, which is why the FCI's own misconception taxonomy maps onto these entries directly.
canonical_explanation: Both balls reach the ground at the same time, because the extra gravitational pull on the heavier ball is exactly offset by its greater resistance to being accelerated.
answer_giveaway_terms: hit the ground at the same time

misconceptions.name: Heavier things fall faster
misconceptions.belief: Heavy stuff falls faster than light stuff. Gravity has to pull harder on something heavy, that is what makes it heavy, so it gets yanked down quicker. A brick drops way faster than a bit of paper and you have seen that a hundred times. So if one ball weighs twice as much, gravity is pulling on it twice as hard and it gets down there first.
misconceptions.predicts: The heavier ball hits the ground first, by enough that you would see it or hear two separate thuds rather than one. Pushed for a number, twice the weight means about half the fall time.
changes_only_when: you go up somewhere high yourself with two things of different weights, drop them, and listen for whether it is one thud or two
you get to compare two things that are exactly the same size and shape, so you cannot put it down to the air
someone makes you say what happens if you tape the two balls together, and your own rule gives you two answers that do not match
misconceptions.slides_into: That the Earth pulls on everything the same, so the lighter ball, having less to shift, speeds up more and lands first instead.

misconceptions.name: Things fall because they are heavy
misconceptions.belief: Things fall because they are heavy. That is the reason, and the heaviness is in the thing itself. Nothing has to pull it. Something really light, like a feather, is not heavy enough to fall properly, which is why it drifts instead. So the heavier ball has more of what makes things go down.
misconceptions.predicts: The heavier ball goes down more, and lands first. Asked what makes it fall, you do not name anything outside the ball itself; you point back at its weight.
changes_only_when: you have to explain what makes a scrunched-up crisp packet fall when it hardly weighs anything at all
someone asks you what is doing the pulling, and that your answer is not an answer to that question
you have to say what changed for something that was falling and then stopped, or floated
misconceptions.slides_into: That there is something outside the object doing the pulling, but that it only really works on heavy things and barely bothers with light ones.

misconceptions.name: Gravity gets stronger the closer to the ground you are
misconceptions.belief: Gravity is not the same the whole way down. Up on the roof you are further away so the pull is weaker, and the closer you get to the ground the harder it grabs you. That is why things speed up as they fall instead of going down at one steady speed, and it is why there is none of it out in space.
misconceptions.predicts: The heavier ball wins and the gap opens up as they fall, so they start out close together and the heavy one pulls away near the bottom. Drop them from higher and the difference should be bigger.
changes_only_when: you have to put actual numbers on how much the pull changes between the roof and one metre lower down
you drop the same thing off a low shelf and off a high roof and compare how much it speeds up in the first bit of each fall
someone points at how far away the Moon is and asks what is keeping it going round
misconceptions.slides_into: That it is an air thing, and it stops wherever the air stops, which is why there is none in space.

misconceptions.name: Things fall at one steady speed set by their weight
misconceptions.belief: A falling thing gets going and then just drops at its own speed the rest of the way. Its speed depends on how much it weighs, and its weight does not change while it is falling, so its speed does not either. The heavy ball has a bigger steady speed and the light one a smaller one.
misconceptions.predicts: Each ball has its own fixed drop speed set by its weight, so the heavy one beats the light one by the same ratio whatever height you drop from, and doubling the height exactly doubles both times.
changes_only_when: you film a drop and count how far it moves in each chunk of time
you compare how hard the same thing lands from a first-floor window and from a roof
you have to say what the speed is at the instant you let go, if the speed is already set by the weight
misconceptions.slides_into: That it does speed up, but only because the pull itself gets stronger further down.
